toolDefinitions.description:
runCode is an isolated JavaScript runtime that runs one snippet and returns what
that snippet returns — use it for any computation (arithmetic, string work,
dates, sorting, reshaping JSON) and for this session's functions, which it
exposes under `tools.*`. The runtime is JavaScriptCore, core JavaScript only:
`import` and `require` do not exist, there are no modules and no node, deno or
bun APIs, and every function you can call is under `tools.*`. Write one snippet
calling the exact `tools.*` paths searchTools returned, await every call, and
`return` the final value; only that value comes back. Awaiting a call is the
whole of how a snippet coordinates its work: do not wait() inside a snippet, and
never time a call or poll for one. When runCode answers with `pending` false, the
snippet is done and its result is the detail field: answer from that result. When
runCode answers with `pending` true, the snippet is still going.
Its result will arrive in this conversation as a message when it is ready. You do not need to wait for it or check on it, and no tool can make it come sooner. Go on with any work that does not need it. If none is left, post your status as plain text: what you wait on and its completion token. Answer only from what the snippet returns: never
state a fact about the user's data that did not come from a `tools.*` return
value, and never claim success for a call the snippet did not actually return.
When a snippet fails, fix it and call runCode again immediately. Ambient globals never appear in searchTools — run `docs("globals")` in a snippet to read them.

toolDefinitions.description:
This session's functions are mounted dynamically, and searchTools is the only
way to see them. Call searchTools before you answer any request, passing the
user's own request as the query; describe the task in plain language and you
get back the relevant tool-functions, each with its typed signature, purpose,
and a runnable example. Search again for every further capability the request
needs, and say so and name the capability when nothing relevant comes back.
Never name a function yourself, and never ask the user for data a function can
fetch.
toolDefinitions.name: searchTools
toolDefinitions.parametersSchemaJSON: {"additionalProperties":false,"properties":{"task":{"description":"Describe the task in plain language. Returns the tool-functions for that task, each with its typed signature and a runnable example.","type":"string"}},"required":["task"],"title":"SearchToolsArguments","type":"object","x-order":["task"]}

toolDefinitions.description:
Skills are procedures for kinds of work. Each one tells you how to do the work and which tools to use.
Read the skills below before you start. If a skill helps with any part of your task, load it now: call this tool with {"op": "use skill", "id": "<id>"}. Load each skill that helps. More than one can apply. The answer is the text of the skill. Do the work the way it says. Read this list again when the work changes.
A skill can have files, such as references/guide.md. To read one, call the `skills` tool with {"op": "read resource", "id": "<id>", "path": "<path relative to the skill>"}. The answer of `use skill` lists the files of the skill.

- code: Use this skill when presented with a coding task.
- code-analyzing: Use to find and search code symbols, definitions, references, usage, and impact. Also use early in a session to find the project types and how to build, test, or format them.
- code-commit: Use when the user says "commit", "save changes", or "check in", and after each step that works. Use this skill, not raw git commands.
- code-debugging: Use when a test fails, a build fails, or the code does not do what it must do. Find the root cause before you change code.
- code-map: Use when the user says "map", "architecture", or "overview", or wants the structure of the codebase. Writes ARCHITECTURE.md with Mermaid diagrams.
- code-tdd: Use before you write code for a feature, a bug fix, a refactor, or a change of behavior. Write a test that fails, then write the code that makes it pass.
- code-test: Use when the user wants to run tests, or after a code change. Takes a scope (named tests, unit, integration, or project), or finds the scope from the change. Runs the tests and analyzes the results.
- kanban: Use to read or change the kanban board with the `tools.kanban` tool, for example to add, find, assign, move, or update a task. Tells how to use the tool.

toolDefinitions.description:
This tool sends messages. To send a message to a run, call the tool "agents" with the arguments {"op": "send agent", "id": "<id>", "message": "<the message>"}. The value of "op" is an operation of the tool "agents", not the name of a tool. You continue to work after the message is sent.

The session that started you has the id 01M6JKRZA4NJBNESVN3DV9T2KY. Send a message to it with {"op": "send caller", "message": "..."}.
toolDefinitions.name: agents
